segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I, Paul, appeal to you myself by the gentleness and forbearance of Christ—I who am lowly when face to face among you, but bold toward you when absent!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I beg you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence with which I count on daring to confront certain people who count us as walking according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the weapons of our warfare are not weapons of the flesh but are powerful through God for tearing down strongholds. We tear down arguments

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and every lofty obstacle raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we stand ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look at what is in front of you. If anyone is confident of belonging to Christ, let that person consider once more that just as he belongs to Christ, so do we.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be put to shame.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not want to seem as though I am trying to frighten you with my letters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For someone says,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let such a person consider this: what we are in word by letter when absent, we are also in deed when present.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, show no understanding.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the field that God allotted us as our measure—to reach even as far as you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you; we did come even as far as you with the good news of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We do not boast beyond measure, in the labors of others, but we have hope that, as your faith grows, we will be greatly enlarged among you, in keeping with our field,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that we may bring the good news to the regions beyond you, and not boast in someone else’s field about work already done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

notes.note: The traditional pairing is “meekness and gentleness.” “Meek” now suggests weakness, which the first Greek word does not; “gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering. The second word (epieikeia) describes someone with authority who does not insist on the full letter of their rights, so “forbearance” is used here; “clemency” or “kindness” are also defensible.

Paul is almost certainly echoing a taunt made against him in Corinth (compare verse 10): unimpressive and submissive in person, bold only from a distance. In ordinary Greek usage this word was often an insult, meaning low in status or servile, though Jewish and Christian writers also used it positively for humility. Paul repeats the jibe with irony.

“Flesh” in Paul often means human nature left to its own resources and motives. To “walk according to the flesh” is to conduct oneself by merely human standards, which is the charge his critics made; in verse 3 he plays on the word, granting that he lives “in the flesh” as an ordinary mortal while denying that he fights by its methods.

The Greek is simply “powerful to God” or “powerful for God.” It may mean powerful by God’s agency, powerful in God’s service, or, as a Semitic-style intensive, “divinely powerful.” The rendering here follows the first reading, which is traditional, but the others are well supported.

notes.phrase: Look at what is in front of you.
notes.traditional: Do ye look on things after the outward appearance?
notes.note: The Greek verb form can be a command (“Look at what is in front of you”), a statement (“You are looking only at appearances”), or a question (“Are you looking only at appearances?”). The command is chosen here because Paul normally uses this form as an imperative, but translations are divided. The phrase rendered “in front of you” is the same one translated “face to face” in verse 1.

The Greek verb is singular, “he says.” It may refer to one particular critic at Corinth, which fits “such a person” in verse 11, or it may be used loosely in the manner of “people say” or “it is said.”

A few manuscripts of the Western tradition lack the words “show no understanding. We, however,” at the end of verse 12 and the start of verse 13, so that it is Paul who measures himself by himself. The longer reading, translated here, is far better attested and is followed by nearly all modern editions.

The word (kanōn) basically means a measuring rod and so a rule or standard. Here and in verses 15–16 most modern interpreters take it to mean the area of work God assigned to Paul, hence “field,” “sphere” or “territory.” Others keep the sense “standard” or “limit.” The geographical language of reaching “as far as you” and “the regions beyond you” favors the former, but the matter is disputed.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

notes.phrase: we will be greatly enlarged among you
notes.traditional: we shall be enlarged by you
notes.note: The verb means to be made great or to be magnified. Paul may mean that his sphere of work will be widened with the Corinthians’ help, which fits the next verse, or that he will be held in greater honor among them. The Greek phrase rendered “among you” could also mean “by you.”

notes.phrase: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”
notes.note: Paul gives no citation formula, but the words are a condensed form of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Septuagint). He quotes the same line in 1 Corinthians 1:31, where he introduces it with “as it is written.”

candidates.reason: Paul’s uses range from the physical body to human nature opposed to God, and translations vary widely between “flesh,” “human standards,” “sinful nature” and “world”; a reader needs one policy.
The Semitic idiom of “walking” for conduct recurs throughout the letters and John, and translations split between “walk” and “live.”
A key Pauline word group rendered variously as “boast,” “glory,” “take pride” and “exult,” sometimes positive and sometimes negative; variation obscures the thread.
The word group moves between low social status, an insult, and the virtue of humility across the New Testament, and “humble” does not fit every case.
Recurs heavily in Paul (especially Romans 4) as “reckon,” “count,” “credit” and “consider,” and his wordplay depends on recognizable repetition.
